title: Locations with aggregate AirNow reporting areas (e.g. Boston) never decode -- permanent Data Unavailable
description:
PollutantReading declared siteID, siteName, and lookupBoundary as non-optional String. AirNow returns null for all three whenever a reporting area aggregates across several monitors instead of naming one specific site ('lookupBehavior': 'Highest Reading From Assigned Sites'). Because Codable synthesis fails on a null for a non-optional field, the ENTIRE response fails to decode -- not just those fields -- so such a location shows 'Data Unavailable' forever.

Confirmed against live responses on 2026-08-05 (dev backend, same request shape):
  Boston  (42.36,-71.06): "siteID": null, "siteName": null, "lookupBoundary": null, lookupBehavior='Highest Reading From Assigned Sites'  -> decode FAILS
  Chicago (41.88,-87.63): "siteID": "170310057", "siteName": "CHI_SP"                                                                      -> decode OK

Affects BOTH data-source modes and BOTH processes -- PollutantReading is the shared decode target for AirNowDirectClient and BluegullServiceClient alike, so this is not specific to the widget or to the mtm.23 spike; the container app hits it identically. Found incidentally while instrumenting the mtm.23 widget-fetch spike, which logged: FETCH FAILED in 1.197s -- decodingFailed("The data couldn't be read because it is missing.") for Boston.

P0 because it is silent, permanent, user-visible data loss for an unknown fraction of US metro areas, and Steve hit it on the second real location he tried.
acceptance_criteria: siteID, siteName, and lookupBoundary are optional; a response with nulls for them decodes successfully and displays normally (nothing renders these fields today). Add a regression test decoding a real aggregate-reporting-area payload shaped like the live Boston response. Verify a widget/menu bar pinned to Boston shows a real AQI.
close_reason: Fixed: made siteID, siteName, and lookupBoundary optional on PollutantReading. AirNow returns null for all three on aggregate reporting areas (lookupBehavior 'Highest Reading From Assigned Sites'), and a null against a non-optional Codable field made the ENTIRE payload undecodable, so those locations showed Data Unavailable permanently in both modes and both processes. Added testDecodesAggregateReportingAreaWithNullSiteFields using the verbatim shape of the live 2026-08-05 Boston Metro response. Nothing in the UI reads these fields, so no display change. Verified end-to-end: Boston Metro now decodes and caches (AQI 39). make test-swift passes, 170 BluegullAQIKit tests + 12 BluegullAQITests.

title: Re-review AirNow Data Exchange Guidelines for commercial/monetized use
description: The 2026-07-28 AirNow terms review (bluegull-aqi-8ef.10) approved Service mode caching/redistribution, but explicitly flagged 'No explicit commercial-use clause, no App Store-specific restriction' as unresolved (doc/DESIGN.md "Not found / would need registration to check further"). Steve has now decided to pivot from non-profit to a for-profit model that collects money to cover infrastructure costs and pay himself for ongoing operations. That changes the compliance picture materially -- redistributing EPA/AirNow data as part of a monetized product is a different question than free/non-profit redistribution, and the prior sign-off didn't cover it. Re-review the Data Exchange Guidelines, API FAQ, and Fact Sheet specifically for commercial-use language, and consider whether this needs to be raised directly with AirNow (dmc@airnowtech.org) before launch -- see DESIGN.md's threat model priority #2: losing the AirNow key/quota takes the whole service down and can't be fixed by scaling.
acceptance_criteria: Either a clear compliance answer (commercial use is permitted under the existing guidelines, with citation) or a decision to proactively contact AirNow before monetizing, documented in doc/DESIGN.md.
close_reason: Resolved: proceed under the existing 2026-07-28 Service-mode approval, no proactive disclosure of commercial status to AirNow. Re-confirmed directly (not just re-asserted) that the Data Exchange Guidelines, FAQ, and registration form are genuinely silent on commercial use. Found Domo's commercial 'AirNow Connector' as real (if imperfect) evidence AirNow tolerates commercial products on their API -- initial BYO-key-based skepticism was miscalibrated (conflated an already-resolved redistribution question with the actually-open commercial-tolerance question); corrected after Steve's pushback. Documented in doc/DESIGN.md 'Commercial use re-review'.

title: Review AirNow API terms of use for compliance
description:
Research complete 2026-07-27; decision made 2026-07-28. See doc/DESIGN.md 'AirNow terms review -- research findings' for the full writeup.

OPERATIVE AGREEMENT: no separate API ToS; the EPA AirNow Data Exchange Guidelines PDF (docs.airnowapi.org/docs/DataUseGuidelines.pdf, updated Aug 2025) is what registration agrees to. Confirmed by fetching both the registration page and the PDF.

FINDINGS: nothing prohibits redistribution. The API FAQ explicitly endorses the caching pattern this project uses ('cache daily or hourly... populate your own database'), with one caveat (no bulk zip-code enumeration) that opportunistic per-request caching doesn't trigger.

DECISION: caching and redistributing AirNow data via a proxy server is permitted. Service mode proceeds alongside Direct mode.

OBLIGATIONS identified during review -- unaffected by this decision, tracked separately, gating App Store submission rather than the start of implementation:
  1. Two-tier attribution (specific agency first, then AirNow/EPA): 10h.15, e70.10, mtm.14
  2. In-product preliminary-data disclaimer: dc2.4
  3. Official EPA AQI colors, binding via incorporation into the Guidelines: 10h.2
  4. Never derive AQI client-side: 10h.17
  5. Notify AirNow the product exists: 8ef.13
  6. Keep AirNow contact info current: 8ef.14
Full set: bd list --label compliance
close_reason: Reviewed and approved by the project owner 2026-07-28: caching and redistributing AirNow data via a proxy server is permitted, so Service mode proceeds. Unblocks all implementation. Compliance obligations remain tracked under the 'compliance' label and gate App Store submission, not implementation start.

title: Verify CLGeocoder works without the app's location entitlement
description:
hib.6 removed com.apple.security.personal-information.location from the CONTAINER APP (not the helper), on the documented basis that CLGeocoder needs network access rather than location authorization -- see LocationResolver's own doc comment and hib.6's acceptance criterion 'Pinned locations work with no location grant present at all.'

That has never been exercised on a signed, sandboxed build without the entitlement, because the app always had it before. If the claim is wrong, two things break and both are silent-ish: SystemAddressGeocoder.geocode (adding a pinned location by address or zip) and SystemReverseGeocoder.placeName (ResolvedPlaceNameCaption, the 'what did Current Location resolve to' caption).

DO THIS ON THE FIRST SIGNED BUILD, before anything else in the epic gets tested -- it is cheap to check and it decides whether the entitlement has to come back.

HOW: signed build, no location grant anywhere. Settings > add a pinned location by zip code. Expect a resolved coordinate and a reading. Then check ResolvedPlaceNameCaption renders a place name for a cached current-location reading.

IF IT FAILS: restore the entitlement to the app target in project.yml, and update SingleLocationPromptTests.testTheAppHasNoLocationEntitlement -- the source-scan tests still hold the real line (no requestWhenInUseAuthorization outside the helper), which is what actually prevents a second prompt. The entitlement removal is belt, not braces.

title: SPIKE: does an SMAppService agent actually wake on a repeating XPC Activity from cold boot?
description:
Prerequisite evidence for the hib.1 go/no-go. The epic's central lifecycle claim -- "modelled on weatherd: MachServices + EnablePressuredExit + EnableTransactions + XPC Activity, NO RunAtLoad, NO KeepAlive, entire lifecycle is public API" -- has a bootstrap hole nobody has tested.

THE HOLE: hib.5 registers the periodic activity with xpc_activity_register, which is code that only runs while the helper is already running. hib.3 gives the plist no RunAtLoad and no KeepAlive. hib.3 also establishes that the widget extension cannot start the helper, and the whole premise is that the main app may never be launched. So after a reboot with the app never launched, nothing invokes the MachService and no code has run to register any activity. Nothing starts the helper. Ever.

It closes only if one of these is true, and neither is documented:
  (a) launchd persists an xpc_activity_register'd activity for a third-party on-demand agent across process exit AND across reboot, and relaunches the job when the activity fires; or
  (b) the plist itself can carry LaunchEvents -> com.apple.xpc.activity (with Repeating=true) and SMAppService honours it on registration.

On (b): SMAppService.h in the current SDK promises only "the standard launchd.plist keys" plus BundleProgram. It is silent on LaunchEvents. weatherd DOES use LaunchEvents -> com.apple.xpc.activity -- but weatherd is an Apple system agent installed directly in /System/Library/LaunchAgents, never registered through SMAppService, so it is no evidence either way. (Also note weatherd's own activity is Repeating=false; weatherd's actual freshness comes from push -- MachServices com.apple.aps.weather + LaunchEvents com.apple.nsurlsessiond-events. We have no push channel.)

WHAT TO BUILD: minimal signed sandboxed LSUIElement helper, FRESH bundle id (see hib.2 -- the 2026-08-12 grant on solutions.bluegull.aqi.helper is unremovable). No AQI work, no CoreLocation. Just os_log a line with a timestamp on every wake. Register it from a throwaway container app via SMAppService.agent. Try variant (b) first (LaunchEvents in the plist, short GracePeriod for test turnaround) and variant (a) second (xpc_activity_register in code).

QUESTIONS TO ANSWER:
1. Does SMAppService.agent even accept a plist containing LaunchEvents, or does register() throw / silently drop the key?
2. Does the helper get woken periodically with the container app QUIT?
3. Does it survive a reboot -- log out, reboot, do NOT launch the container app, wait past one interval, check the log?
4. Does it actually exit between wakes (EnablePressuredExit + EnableTransactions), or does it linger, in which case it is a resident process and hib.1's Option 3 has lost its main advantage over Option 2?
5. Bonus, cheap while set up: launch the helper headless via launchd with NO location grant and see whether a permission prompt appears at all and what it is attributed to. The 2026-08-12 spike never covered this case, and under hib.6 (helper as sole location owner) it IS the entire first-run experience.

IF THE ANSWER IS NO: Option 3 as designed does not exist. The fallback is a KeepAlive agent, which is a resident background process -- i.e. Option 2 with an extra bundle, extra TCC identity, and extra weeks. That should be decided knowingly, not discovered in hib.5.
acceptance_criteria: A written answer to questions 1-4 backed by log evidence from a real Mac, including at least one reboot cycle with the container app never launched. Recorded on hib.1 so the go/no-go rests on measurement rather than on the weatherd analogy.
close_reason: Closed

comments.author: Steve Barber
comments.text:
QUESTION 1 ANSWERED: YES (2026-08-30, spike/hib10 on branch feat/location-helper-agent).

SMAppService.agent accepts a plist containing LaunchEvents -> com.apple.xpc.activity, and launchd keeps the criteria verbatim rather than silently dropping them. This was the part SMAppService.h is silent about, and it is the load-bearing unknown for the whole epic.

register() returned OK with status=enabled -- note ENABLED, not requiresApproval, on a machine that has previously approved a BlueGull login item.

Confirmed independently rather than trusting the return value, via `launchctl print gui/501/solutions.bluegull.hib10.checkin`:

  event triggers = {
      solutions.bluegull.hib10.checkin.wake => {
          keepalive = 0
          service = solutions.bluegull.hib10.checkin
          stream = com.apple.xpc.activity
          monitor = com.apple.UserEventAgent-Aqua
          descriptor = {
              "Repeating" => true
              "Interval" => 300
              "GracePeriod" => 60
              "AllowBattery" => true
              "Priority" => "Utility"
          }
      }
  }
  event channels = { "com.apple.xpc.activity" = { managed = 1, watching = 1 } }

Every criterion survived registration intact, the stream is bound to com.apple.UserEventAgent-Aqua, and the channel reports watching = 1. Also in that output: `managed_by = com.apple.xpc.ServiceManagement`, a BTM uuid (the Background Task Management record behind the Login Items row), `program identifier = Contents/MacOS/hib10-agent` resolved from BundleProgram, and `parent bundle identifier = solutions.bluegull.hib10.container`.

At the same moment the checkin job reads `state = not running`, `runs = 0`, `active count = 0` -- exactly right. It has NEVER been started, because it has no RunAtLoad and no KeepAlive. Whether launchd starts it on the activity's account is questions 2-4, still in flight.

SUPPORTING EVIDENCE FOUND IN THE SDK (this is why variant B was made the primary hypothesis rather than a long shot): xpc/activity.h documents XPC_ACTIVITY_CHECK_IN as checking in "with the system for previously registered activity using the same identifier (for example, AN ACTIVITY TAKEN FROM A LAUNCHD PROPERTY LIST)". Plist-declared XPC activities are a documented, supported mechanism; the only open part was whether SMAppService specifically preserved them. It does.

CORRECTION TO hib.5 while in the header: RequireNetworkConnectivity, which weatherd sets and hib.5 proposes copying, is NOT a public XPC activity constant. It does not appear in xpc/activity.h at all. It can be written into a plist (weatherd does) but cannot be set from xpc_dictionary_set_* against a documented key, and it is not contract. The public criteria constants are Interval, Repeating, Delay, GracePeriod, Priority (Maintenance|Utility), AllowBattery, RequireScreenSleep, PreventsDeviceSleep, RequireHDDSpinning. Public interval constants run 1/5/15/30 min, 1/4/8 hours, 1/7 days -- so an hourly refresh is a first-class supported cadence.

SETUP NOTES worth keeping for whoever builds the real helper:
- The agent is a `tool` target with CREATE_INFOPLIST_SECTION_IN_BINARY, giving it its own CFBundleIdentifier (solutions.bluegull.hib10.agent) embedded in the Mach-O and its own code-signing identifier, distinct from the container's. Confirmed via codesign -dv on the embedded copy. That separate identity is the whole premise behind hib.6's "needs its own grant".
- Two traps produced a signed-but-unsandboxed agent that looked fine until the signature was inspected. (a) xcodegen GENERATES the file named by `entitlements: path:` and overwrites it -- a hand-written entitlements file with only a path becomes an empty <dict/> on the next generate. Entitlements must be under `properties:`, as mac-app/project.yml already does. (b) Xcode's ProcessProductPackaging filters entitlements against a provisioning profile, and manual Developer ID signing has none, so it dropped app-sandbox and left only get-task-allow. The spike's `make build` now signs by hand inside-out and prints the resulting entitlements so this cannot slip through silently.
- Signed Developer ID, not Apple Development. Higher fidelity, not laziness: TCC/locationd grants pin to the signing identity, so the shipping identity is the right one to test under.
- Installed to /Applications, not run from DerivedData: SMAppService records the app path at registration, and DerivedData paths move with the checkout path -- the same trap bluegull-aqi-mtm.9 documents for widget registration.

comments.author: Steve Barber
comments.text:
QUESTION 2 ANSWERED: YES -- and this is the epic's central lifecycle claim demonstrated rather than assumed (2026-08-30 16:40:02 local).

launchd started the checkin agent FROM NOTHING, on the plist-declared activity's account alone. Verbatim:

  16:37:30  Hib10Container   register solutions.bluegull.hib10.checkin: OK status=enabled
  16:37:30  Hib10Container   [container process exits]
  ...
  16:40:02  hib10-agent[8014]  PROCESS_START pid=8014 ppid=1 mode=checkin
  16:40:02  hib10-agent[8014]  REGISTER_CHECK_IN pid=8014 activity=...checkin.wake
  16:40:02  hib10-agent[8014]  ACTIVITY_CHECK_IN pid=8014 -- criteria came from the launchd plist
  16:40:02  hib10-agent[8014]  ACTIVITY_RUN pid=8014 wake=1 secs_since_process_start=0
  16:40:04  hib10-agent[8014]  ACTIVITY_DONE pid=8014 wake=1 -- transaction ended

Every condition the epic depends on held at once: no RunAtLoad, no KeepAlive, the agent had NEVER run before (launchctl showed runs=0 immediately after registration), and the container app had already exited two and a half minutes earlier. ppid=1 is launchd. secs_since_process_start=0 means the process was spawned specifically to service the activity, not spawned for some other reason and handed the activity afterwards.

The full documented flow works end to end: plist declares the activity -> SMAppService preserves it -> launchd watches it -> launchd spawns the agent when it comes due -> agent calls xpc_activity_register with XPC_ACTIVITY_CHECK_IN -> system hands back the plist-declared activity -> RUN -> DONE.

TIMING DETAIL WORTH KEEPING: first fire was 152s after registration, against a 300s Interval. That is not the system being early, it is xpc/activity.h's documented default -- an Interval with no explicit Delay implies "XPC_ACTIVITY_DELAY with a value of half the 'interval'". So the first refresh after install lands at roughly half the cadence, then settles. Relevant to hib.5's cadence design and to first-run UX: an hourly helper would populate the cache ~30 min after install, not ~60.

COALESCING CONFIRMED: both variants fired at the same instant (16:40:02.1), despite being independent jobs with independent activities. That is the OS batching work, which is exactly the behaviour hib.5 was counting on when it argued a grace period lets the system coalesce our refresh with other activity.

QUESTION 4 -- PRELIMINARY, NOT YET FINAL: both agents were still alive at 16:43, three minutes after ACTIVITY_DONE ended their transactions, with EnablePressuredExit=true and EnableTransactions=true set. So "exits when idle" is looking like NO. Worth being precise about why rather than calling it a bug: pressured exit means the process becomes ELIGIBLE to be killed when the system wants the memory, not that launchd reaps it promptly on going idle. If that holds up across the next few wakes (watch for the pid on ACTIVITY_RUN changing -- same pid means it never left), then Option 3's "genuinely on-demand lifecycle, exits when idle" advantage over Option 2 is materially weaker than hib.1 assumes: in practice it is a resident background process that is merely small. Still measuring.

comments.author: Steve Barber
comments.text:
QUESTIONS 2 AND 4 FINAL (2026-08-30, 23 minutes / 5 wake cycles observed, container app never running after 16:37:30).

QUESTION 2 -- DOES IT WAKE REPEATEDLY WITH THE APP QUIT? YES, reliably.

checkin variant (pid 8014), plist-declared activity, no RunAtLoad, no KeepAlive:
  16:40:02  wake=1   (152s after registration)
  16:45:09  wake=2   +307s
  16:50:55  wake=3   +346s
  16:55:26  wake=4   +271s
  17:00:01  wake=5   +275s

Five for five against a 300s nominal Interval, spread 271-346s -- the GracePeriod=60 slack, exactly as specified. Not a one-off: this is a working repeating schedule with nothing of ours running to maintain it. The register variant (pid 7628) tracked it identically.

Coalescing is real but NOT guaranteed: wakes 1-4 fired within milliseconds of each other across the two independent jobs; at wake 5 they separated by 16 seconds. So hib.5 can count on the OS batching opportunistically, not on it always happening.

QUESTION 4 -- DOES IT EXIT BETWEEN WAKES? NO. This is the finding that costs Option 3 its main advantage.

pid 8014 serviced ALL FIVE wakes. secs_since_process_start climbs 0 -> 307 -> 653 -> 924 -> 1199. Same for pid 7628 across its five. Neither process was ever reaped; no PROCESS_EXIT line was ever written, meaning neither ever received SIGTERM. This is with EnablePressuredExit=true, EnableTransactions=true, ProcessType=Adaptive, and the agent correctly bracketing its work in xpc_transaction_begin/end and calling xpc_activity_set_state(DONE) -- i.e. the agent did everything the epic's design says to do, and launchd still kept it resident.

Being precise about why, because it is not a bug: "pressured exit" means the process becomes ELIGIBLE for termination when the system wants the memory. It does not mean launchd reaps an idle job promptly. On an unpressured machine the agent simply stays.

WHAT IT ACTUALLY COSTS TO STAY: measured, 2.9 MB phys_footprint (RSS 5.2 MB), 0.0% CPU idle. So "resident" here is genuinely cheap.

CONSEQUENCE FOR hib.1, stated plainly. The epic's framing was that Option 3 "buys a genuinely on-demand lifecycle (exits when idle, system-scheduled wakeups via XPC Activity)" versus Option 2's resident app. Half of that is now measured true and half measured false:
  - System-scheduled wakeups: REAL, and they work with the app quit. This is the genuine win, and it is not available to Option 2 at all.
  - Exits when idle: NOT what happens. In practice it is a resident background process too -- just a 2.9 MB one instead of a full SwiftUI menu bar app.

So the honest comparison is no longer "on-demand helper vs resident app". It is "a 2.9 MB resident helper that the OS schedules, vs a resident menu bar app that schedules itself" -- both permanently resident, both one row in Login Items & Extensions, and the remaining difference is footprint plus who owns the timer. That is a real difference and it is smaller than hib.1's Option 3 description implies. Worth correcting the epic's own text either way.

STILL OPEN: question 3, the reboot test, which needs a human. Cannot be answered from here.

comments.author: Steve Barber
comments.text:
QUESTION 4 CORROBORATED FROM LAUNCHD'S OWN COUNTERS (30-minute sampling of `launchctl print`, every 60s).

Independent of parsing our own os_log lines, launchd's job state agrees: across the entire window both jobs held

  runs = 1
  last exit code = (never exited)
  state = running

The checkin job stepped runs = 0 -> runs = 1 at its single cold start (16:40:02) and never moved again, through five ACTIVITY_RUN cycles. launchd never counted a second launch because there was never a second launch -- and "last exit code = (never exited)" is launchd stating outright that the process never terminated.

So the agent does not exit between wakes, confirmed two independent ways: our own pid staying constant across wakes, and launchd's own run counter and exit record. Not a logging artifact.

comments.author: Steve Barber
comments.text:
CORRECTION TO QUESTION 4, plus a strong partial answer to QUESTION 3. Observed 2026-08-31 after ~29 hours unattended. No reboot occurred (uptime 1 day 1:12, boot Aug 30 15:58), so question 3 proper is still open -- but the machine produced the next best thing on its own.

WHAT HAPPENED: 247 wakes over ~29 hours, uninterrupted, container app never launched again after the initial registration.

pid 8014 (checkin) ran from 2026-08-30 16:40 to 2026-08-31 12:11, serving 224 consecutive wakes over 19.5 hours. Then:

  launchctl print gui/501/solutions.bluegull.hib10.checkin
      runs = 2
      last exit reason = JETSAM_REASON_MEMORY_IDLE_EXIT

  12:11:19  ACTIVITY_DONE pid=8014 wake=224     <- last sign of the old process
  [killed by jetsam; SIGKILL, so no PROCESS_EXIT line was ever written]
  12:15:55  PROCESS_START pid=51857 ppid=1 mode=checkin
  12:15:55  ACTIVITY_RUN  pid=51857 wake=1 secs_since_process_start=0

SO QUESTION 4'S ANSWER IS NOT "NO", IT IS "YES BUT ON THE SYSTEM'S SCHEDULE, NOT PER-WAKE". My earlier reading, taken from a 23-minute window, said the agent never exits. Over a day it does: EnablePressuredExit works, and the exit reason names it explicitly (MEMORY_IDLE_EXIT). What it does not do is exit after each wake. The real lifecycle is: resident for hours at ~2.9 MB, reaped by jetsam when the system wants idle memory back, then re-spawned on the next activity firing.

That is a better result for the epic than "never exits", and still not the "starts when needed, exits when idle" the epic describes. Both descriptions were wrong; this is the measured one.

QUESTION 3, PARTIALLY ANSWERED IN SPIRIT: the relaunch at 12:15:55 is a COLD start of an agent whose process was gone, driven purely by the activity, with the container app not running -- PROCESS_START immediately followed by ACTIVITY_RUN wake=1 at secs_since_process_start=0. So the activity registration survives the death of the process and launchd re-spawns from nothing. What is still untested is whether it survives a REBOOT, which is a different store (launchd's on-disk job state vs its live state). Lower risk than it looked yesterday, but not the same question.

DESIGN CONSEQUENCE FOR hib.4, worth acting on regardless of the hib.1 outcome: the kill is SIGKILL, not SIGTERM. launchctl list showed status -9 and no PROCESS_EXIT line was ever logged despite a SIGTERM handler being installed. A real helper therefore CANNOT rely on a clean-shutdown hook to flush anything. Every App Group cache write has to be atomic and safe to be interrupted at any instant, because the process can vanish mid-operation with no warning and no signal it can catch.

comments.author: Steve Barber
comments.text:
QUESTION 3 ANSWERED: YES. All four questions are now closed. (2026-08-31, reboot at 17:14:45.)

Reboot performed, container app NEVER launched afterwards.

  17:14:45  system boot
  17:16:05  hib10-agent pid=1852 starts -- this is the REGISTER variant, RunAtLoad, at login. Proves nothing on its own; it is the control.
  17:20:06  hib10-agent pid=2443 ppid=1 starts -- the CHECKIN variant. No RunAtLoad. No KeepAlive. Nothing of ours running.
  17:20:06  ACTIVITY_RUN pid=2443 wake=1 secs_since_process_start=0

Five minutes twenty-one seconds after boot, launchd spawned an agent that had no RunAtLoad, no KeepAlive, and no running container app, purely because a plist-declared XPC activity came due. secs_since_process_start=0 means the process was created to service the activity rather than started for some other reason and handed it afterwards.

THE CONTROL DISCRIMINATES CLEANLY, which is why both variants were worth carrying: the register variant's own wake=1 logged secs_since_process_start=233 -- it was already resident (RunAtLoad put it there at login) when the activity fired. The checkin variant logged 0. Same activity mechanism, opposite process histories, and the design that matters is the one that started from nothing.

Criteria confirmed intact after the reboot, before any wake, via launchctl print: the full event triggers block restored with Interval 300, GracePeriod 60, Repeating true, AllowBattery true, Priority Utility, stream com.apple.xpc.activity, monitor com.apple.UserEventAgent-Aqua. So it is launchd's on-disk job state that carries this across a boot, not just live state.

Five wakes in the first 20 minutes post-boot: 17:20:06, 17:22:49, 17:25:57, 17:29:12, 17:35:19 -- spacing 163/188/195/367s against a 300s nominal Interval. Notably tighter than the pre-reboot run averaged; the system appears to fire more eagerly while catching up after boot, then settle. Cadence is a target the OS honours loosely, not a guarantee, which is the correct expectation to design to anyway.

MEASUREMENT GOTCHA WORTH RECORDING FOR hib.9's verification script: for roughly 20 minutes after a reboot, `log show --last 30m` returned ZERO lines for every subsystem, including a no-predicate sanity check -- while `log show --start "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS"` over the same window returned everything. The relative-time form silently returns an empty result rather than an error. This nearly produced a false negative on the single most important measurement in this spike: launchctl said the job was running with runs=1 while the log appeared completely empty. Anyone writing hib.9's post-reboot checklist should use --start with an absolute time, and should cross-check against `ps -o lstart` and `launchctl print` rather than trusting the log alone.

SPIKE COMPLETE. Summary of all four:
  1. Does SMAppService.agent accept LaunchEvents -> com.apple.xpc.activity?  YES, criteria preserved verbatim.
  2. Does it wake with the container app quit?                               YES, 247 wakes over 29 hours.
  3. Does it survive a reboot with the app never launched?                   YES, cold start 5m21s after boot.
  4. Does it exit between wakes?                                             NOT per-wake. Resident for ~19.5 hours at 2.9 MB, then reaped by JETSAM_REASON_MEMORY_IDLE_EXIT and re-spawned on the next activity.

comments.author: Steve Barber
comments.text:
QUESTION 5 ANSWERED: YES -- a headless, launchd-started helper CAN get a location grant on first run. Measured 2026-09-01 15:07:30, on a fresh single-use bundle id.

  15:07:30.765  PROBE_START pid=59824 ppid=1 bundle=solutions.bluegull.hib10.locprobe1
  15:07:30.768  STATUS_BEFORE notDetermined(0) servicesEnabled=true
  15:07:30.768  REQUESTING_AUTHORIZATION
  15:07:30.815  AUTH_CHANGED notDetermined(0) after=0.2s   <- prompt drawn, CoreLocationAgent live
  15:07:36.045  AUTH_CHANGED authorizedAlways(3) after=5.4s <- Steve clicked Allow
  15:07:36.052  GOT_FIX accuracy=35m after=5.4s

Every condition that makes this the real question held simultaneously: ppid=1 (launchd started it, not a human), no RunAtLoad on the job, the container app not running, a bundle id never seen by locationd before, and a verified notDetermined starting status. CoreLocation engaged fully -- delegate callbacks fired within 0.2s -- which is the sharpest possible contrast with the widget extension, where authStatus stayed 0 with delegateCallbacks=0 and CoreLocation never engaged at all.

CONSEQUENCE: hib.6's ownership inversion IS buildable. The gate this spike was created to test is cleared, and the last mechanical unknown in the epic is gone.

EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN NOTE, since the result is load-bearing: the probe was deliberately built as an LSUIElement .app with a real Info.plist, NOT as a bare `tool` target like the other two spike agents. That reuses the exact bundle shape the 2026-08-12 spike proved works when user-launched, so the only variable changed was who starts the process. Had a bare tool failed to prompt, "headless processes cannot prompt" would have been indistinguishable from "an embedded __info_plist section is not read for usage descriptions" -- and with one shot per bundle id, an ambiguous result would have been a wasted experiment.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT PROVE, and it matters for the product rather than the mechanism:

1. TIMING IS UNCONTROLLED, AND THAT IS A REAL UX PROBLEM. The prompt appeared ~70 seconds after registration because the activity Interval was set to 60s for turnaround, and because a human had been told to watch for it. In the shipping design the helper fires on the SYSTEM's schedule -- possibly hours after install, possibly mid-task, from a process the user does not recognise, with no context for why they are being asked. "A prompt appears" and "a prompt appears at a moment the user understands" are different claims and only the first is measured. The fix is available (have the app start the helper deliberately at the moment the user enables Current Location, rather than letting the first activity firing surprise them) but it is design work that hib.6 does not currently mention.

2. THE PROMPT CARRIES THE HELPER'S NAME, NOT THE APP'S. This one said "BlueGull AQI Location Probe" because that is the probe's CFBundleDisplayName. A shipping helper needs a display name the user recognises as BlueGull AQI, or the prompt reads as coming from something unfamiliar. Cheap to get right, easy to overlook.

3. A HELPER AWAITING A PROMPT MUST HOLD A TRANSACTION. This probe never called xpc_transaction_begin, so between the request and the user's answer launchd considered the job idle and reapable. It survived only because Steve answered in 5.4 seconds. A real user might take a minute. The first-run path specifically has to keep a transaction open across an unbounded human decision -- which sits in direct tension with the pressured-exit design everywhere else, and belongs in hib.4's implementation notes.

HOUSEKEEPING: solutions.bluegull.hib10.locprobe1 is now SPENT -- it holds an unremovable authorizedAlways grant. The probe's own guard caught this correctly on its next three firings (ABORT ... this identifier is spent), and exiting non-zero put launchd into a ~10s respawn retry, so the job was unregistered immediately after the result was captured. A genuine re-run means bumping the numeric suffix in project.yml; there is no other reset.

title: Automate publishing the GitHub Release (DMG + release notes) as a make target
description: For v0.1.0 and v0.1.1, publishing the GitHub Release (attaching mac-app/build/BluegullAQI.dmg from 'make app-package' and using the matching version's section of doc/ReleaseNotes.md as the release body) was done by hand: awk-extract the '## X.Y.Z' section, then 'gh release create vX.Y.Z <dmg> --title vX.Y.Z --notes-file <extracted>'. Steve wants this automated as a make target so it's the first step of the next release rather than a repeated manual sequence.
acceptance_criteria: A new root Makefile target (e.g. 'make github-release') that: (1) reads MARKETING_VERSION from the already-built mac-app/build/export/BluegullAQI.app's Info.plist (not project.yml's fallback) to determine vX.Y.Z; (2) fails with a clear message if mac-app/build/BluegullAQI.dmg doesn't exist yet ('run make app-package first'); (3) fails with a clear message if git tag vX.Y.Z doesn't exist/isn't pushed yet (release notes + tag must already be committed, per the existing commit-notes-before-tag convention); (4) extracts that version's '## X.Y.Z' section from doc/ReleaseNotes.md as the release body, failing clearly if that section is missing; (5) runs gh release create with the DMG attached and that body. Documented in doc/DEVINSTALL.md's 'Package for ad-hoc distribution' section alongside app-package.
close_reason: Added 'make github-release' to the root Makefile: reads MARKETING_VERSION from the built app's own Info.plist, requires the DMG/tag/release-notes-section to already exist (fails clearly naming whichever is missing), extracts the matching '## X.Y.Z' section from doc/ReleaseNotes.md via awk, and runs gh release create. Verified end-to-end against the real v0.1.1 tag/DMG/notes -- reproduced the exact release already published, only stopped by GitHub's own duplicate-tag guard. Documented in doc/DEVINSTALL.md alongside app-package, with the full release sequence (bump version, commit notes, tag+push, app-package, github-release) spelled out.

title: DECISION: go/no-go on the location helper agent
description:
Steve's call, and it gates every other child of this epic. Three options, all costed against evidence rather than speculation:

OPTION 1 -- do nothing. Current Location widgets go stale whenever the menu bar app isn't running. Cost: zero. With dc2.7 + e70.31 shipped the failure is at least honest (absolute timestamp on the widget, no stale number in the menu bar) rather than a silent lie.

OPTION 2 -- make the EXISTING app the resident process. SMAppService.mainApp login item, plus a setting to hide the menu bar icon so 'the menu bar is optional' is satisfied without a second process. The app is already LSUIElement. Cheapest thing that works (~1 day), and it sidesteps the TCC identity problem entirely because it is the bundle that already holds the location grant.

OPTION 3 -- separate helper agent (this epic). Proven viable. Buys a genuinely on-demand lifecycle (exits when idle, system-scheduled wakeups via XPC Activity) and the option of significant-location-change monitoring so data follows the user as they move. Costs weeks, a second TCC identity, and a permanent background-item surface.

KEY EQUIVALENCE worth weighing: options 2 and 3 present the SAME user-visible permission surface -- a row in System Settings > General > Login Items & Extensions, enabled by default, silently revocable by the user. If that cost is being paid either way, the question is only what the extra weeks of option 3 buy.
acceptance_criteria: Steve picks an option and records why. If option 3, the remaining children of this epic are unblocked; if option 1 or 2, this epic is closed or superseded.

comments.author: Steve Barber
comments.text:
Clarification worth keeping in mind before this decision gets made (2026-08-26):

The location helper agent (Option 3) and "the menu bar icon is present automatically after login" are SEPARATE concerns, not the same thing. The helper is headless -- per hib.3's own design, it resolves location, fetches, and writes the App Group cache, but it never shows a menu bar icon and never launches the main app. So even if Option 3 ships in full, the menu bar icon would still only appear when the user manually launches BluegullAQI, unless the main app is ALSO separately made a login item. Only Option 2's mechanism (SMAppService.mainApp) makes the icon itself appear automatically at login -- and that's true regardless of whether Option 3 is also built, since Option 2's own description already anticipates a "hide the menu bar icon" toggle, meaning the resident-app and visible-icon questions are already decoupled from each other in that design.

Practical consequence: if a plain "launch the app at login" toggle (Option 2's core mechanism) ships now, independent of this decision, it isn't a problem for whichever way hib.1 eventually goes:
- If the eventual answer is Option 1 or Option 2, this already IS most of the work.
- If the eventual answer is Option 3, the separate helper agent coexists fine with a login-item main app -- hib.6 (sole location owner) and hib.8 (migration) already need to reconcile "main app may or may not be running/fetching on its own" regardless of whether that running instance was launched manually or via login item, so shipping login-item support now doesn't introduce a new coordination problem, just an existing one that already needed solving.

Worth noting for whoever makes this call later: shipping a plain main-app login item now already realizes a meaningful slice of what Option 2 promises. That's useful real-world signal -- it reframes the eventual hib.1 question from "Option 2 vs Option 3" to "given Option 2's core mechanism already shipped and is working, what does the extra effort of Option 3 additionally buy."

comments.author: Steve Barber
comments.text:
SKEPTICAL DESIGN REVIEW (2026-08-30, branch feat/location-helper-agent). Eleven findings; three of them are load-bearing enough to change the decision.

--- A. The weatherd model is not the model the epic thinks it is ---
Read the actual plist on this Mac (/System/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.weatherd.plist). weatherd's freshness comes from PUSH, not polling: MachServices includes com.apple.aps.weather (Apple Push Notification service) and LaunchEvents includes com.apple.nsurlsessiond-events. Its single XPC activity, com.apple.weatherd.notifications, is Repeating=false, and carries DuetRelatedApplications + RequiresBuddyComplete (private Duet scheduling hooks). So hib.5's "mirror com.apple.weatherd.notifications: GracePeriod 900, AllowBattery, RequireNetworkConnectivity, Priority Utility" copies the parameters of a ONE-SHOT activity onto a job that needs to repeat. weatherd gives us the right shape for an on-demand agent; it does not give us a periodic-refresh mechanism, because it doesn't need one. We have no push channel. We poll.

--- B. Bootstrap gap: with no RunAtLoad and no KeepAlive, who starts the helper the first time? (LOAD-BEARING) ---
hib.5 says register the activity with xpc_activity_register -- code that only runs if the helper is ALREADY running. hib.3 says the plist deliberately has no RunAtLoad and no KeepAlive; hib.3 also notes the widget cannot start it; and the whole point is that the main app may never launch. Cold boot, app never launched: nothing invokes the MachService and no code has run to register the activity. That closes only if either (a) launchd persists a registered XPC activity across reboot for a third-party on-demand agent, or (b) the plist itself carries LaunchEvents -> com.apple.xpc.activity with Repeating=true. Neither is documented. The SMAppService.h header (checked in the current SDK) promises only "the standard launchd.plist keys" plus BundleProgram -- it says nothing about whether LaunchEvents survives SMAppService registration. This single unknown decides whether the epic's central lifecycle claim works at all, and it is currently written up as settled ("whose entire lifecycle is public API", "proven viable"). It is not settled. One day of spike answers it.

--- C. The 2026-08-12 spike proved less than the epic credits it with (LOAD-BEARING) ---
From the bd memory verbatim: (A) helper user-launched via `open` -> prompted, got a fix; (B) helper started headless by launchd WITH THE GRANT ALREADY IN PLACE -> no prompt, got a fix. That proves a separate bundle gets CoreLocation. It does not touch SMAppService registration, on-demand MachService activation, XPC Activity scheduling, or pressured exit. Most importantly it never ran the one case hib.6 depends on entirely: a headless, launchd-started helper with NO grant. Does a permission prompt even appear from a process with no UI and no foreground context? What app name does it attribute to? Under hib.6 the helper is the SOLE location owner, so that untested case IS the whole first-run experience.

--- D. hib.6 and hib.7 contradict each other ---
hib.6 acceptance: "exactly one location permission prompt across a clean install" AND "no AQI fetch originates from the app or the widget for the current-location case." hib.7 fallback: "the app falls back to resolving location itself while it is running." The app can only do that if it holds its own grant -- i.e. a second prompt, or a prompt deferred to the exact moment the user has just discovered background refresh is broken, which is a poor time to ask. One of the two acceptance criteria has to give. Decide it deliberately now rather than discovering it in hib.7.

--- E. XPC Activity does not wake a sleeping Mac ---
Lid closed overnight = no refresh, helper or no helper. And on wake, a resident main app refreshes within seconds anyway. The helper's actual winning window is narrower than the epic implies: Mac awake, app not running.

--- F. The value proposition shrank when v0.2.1 shipped, and shrinks further for an hour's work (LOAD-BEARING) ---
Launch at login shipped (fvt) -- but it is DEFAULT-OFF. LaunchAtLoginToggle.swift only calls SMAppService.mainApp.register() from an explicit user toggle; nothing registers on first launch. Auto-registering mainApp on first launch (opt-out, not opt-in) is about an hour of work and captures most of what Option 3 buys. Per hib.1's own KEY EQUIVALENCE note, it is the same Login Items & Extensions row either way -- the permission cost is already being paid. Do that first, then measure what gap is actually left before spending weeks.

--- G. o3a is a real argument for a helper, but for a much SMALLER helper ---
bluegull-aqi-o3a: cache_delete terminated the menu bar app 7 times in 8 days on Steve's machine, and launch-at-login does not cover mid-session termination. That is the strongest live argument in favour of some resident agent. But the agent that fixes o3a is a watchdog that relaunches the main app -- roughly a day -- not hib.4/5/6/7/8. Two caveats before assuming it: a SANDBOXED helper launching a sibling app bundle via LaunchServices is itself unverified, and the RBSPreventLaunchLimitation in the termination assertion blocks relaunch during the purge, so it needs backoff rather than a respawn loop. Note the circularity: if that watchdog exists and the main app is therefore reliably resident, the location helper's remaining value is close to zero.

--- H. Two bugs the helper would inherit; hib.4 names the less severe one ---
1. (hib.4 has this) SystemLocationProvider.currentLocation() at LocationResolver.swift:100-102 throws .permissionDenied on .notDetermined, microseconds after constructing CLLocationManager. Real race; a short-lived helper hits it.
2. (NOT in any bead) There is NO TIMEOUT on requestLocation(). LocationRequestDelegate (LocationResolver.swift:123/129) resumes the continuation only on didUpdateLocations or didFailWithError. If neither ever arrives -- no fix available, location services wedged -- the continuation never resumes. In a long-lived app that is an invisible hang. In a short-lived helper holding a launchd transaction it means THE PROCESS NEVER EXITS, which destroys the "exits when idle" property that is the entire reason to prefer Option 3 over Option 2. Needs a timeout plus stopUpdatingLocation(), with the continuation guarded against double-resume.

--- I. Running cost, which hib.5 waves at from the wrong side ---
hib.5 defends the AirNow load (grid snapping to ~1.1km, hour-aligned TTLs, 400 cache-miss budget/hour) and that defence holds -- for AirNow. It does not address Lambda invocations, which scale with installs x hours regardless of cache hit rate. Today a fetch only happens when a human is around. A helper polls hourly whether or not anyone is looking. Relevant given q9r.36 (reserved concurrency currently disabled pending a quota increase) and 8ef.16 (App Store revenue is meant to cover the AWS bill).

--- J. First-run testing is one-shot per bundle id, and hib.2 only budgets one ---
hib.2 correctly insists on a fresh bundle id because the 2026-08-12 grant cannot be removed (tccutil has no authority over locationd, fails -10814). But that makes every clean first-run test consume a bundle id. Plus the shipping build is signed Developer ID, a different identity from the dev build's Apple Development leaf, so a dev-obtained grant does not represent the shipping first run anyway. Plan a VM or a spare Mac BEFORE hib.2, or first-run verification stays one-shot forever.

--- K. Minor, but will cost a build cycle ---
hib.2 says "Contents/Library/LaunchAgents (or Contents/MacOS for an SMAppService.agent program)" -- those are conflated. Per SMAppService.h: for agent(plistName:) the PLIST must live in Contents/Library/LaunchAgents, and the executable is referenced by the BundleProgram key as a bundle-relative path. Same header also warns that changing either the plist or the executable requires re-registering (and preferably unregistering first) -- which applies to every dev iteration AND every shipped app update.

--- RECOMMENDATION ---
Do not answer go/no-go yet; two cheap experiments materially change the answer.
1. (B) One-day spike: does an SMAppService-registered agent with LaunchEvents -> com.apple.xpc.activity actually get woken on a repeating schedule, from cold boot, with the main app never launched? If no, Option 3 as designed does not exist and the epic needs redesigning around KeepAlive -- which is just Option 2 with extra steps.
2. (F) One hour: auto-register SMAppService.mainApp on first launch (opt-out). Then observe for a week what freshness gap actually remains.
Current lean: Option 2+ -- auto-register launch-at-login, add the "hide the menu bar icon" setting Option 2 already contemplates, and add an o3a watchdog -- and revisit Option 3 only if measurement shows a real remaining gap. Options 2 and 3 cost the same permission surface; after v0.2.1 the extra weeks buy noticeably less than they did on 2026-08-12.

comments.author: Steve Barber
comments.text:
RECOMMENDATION (2026-08-31, after hib.10 closed). Written up in full at https://claude.ai/code/artifact/bc1d3f3a-d867-4785-855e-1a3182e72368 -- summarised here so the decision record is self-contained.

THE CALL: do not build Option 3 yet. Ship e70.53 (launch-at-login default-on, ~1 hour), measure for a week, and hold Option 3 as a proven, costed option. This is a SEQUENCING call, not a rejection.

WHY SEQUENCING RATHER THAN REJECTION: hib.10 removed every mechanical doubt about Option 3. That cuts against building it now rather than for it -- the option no longer carries technical risk, does not expire, and does not get cheaper by being built today. What hib.10 did NOT remove is the doubt about Option 3's FIRST RUN, and building the mechanism does not touch that.

WHAT THE MEASUREMENT DID TO THE EPIC'S OWN CASE. The epic rests on four claims; two hold, one is refuted, one is untested:
  TRUE      -- background refresh with the app not running. Verified across a reboot. Genuinely unavailable to Option 2 at any price. This is the whole case for Option 3 and it is real.
  TRUE      -- it heals itself after being killed. NEW, and stronger than expected: jetsam killed the agent after 19.5 hours and launchd re-spawned it on the next activity. Neither Option 1 nor Option 2 can do this.
  FALSE     -- "exits when idle / genuinely on-demand lifecycle". It is resident for hours and reaped only when the system wants the memory. So Option 3 is ALSO a permanently resident process, just a 2.9 MB one instead of a full SwiftUI app. This issue's own Option 3 description should be corrected either way.
  UNTESTED  -- that its first run is acceptable. Under hib.6 the helper is the SOLE location owner, so a headless launchd-started process with no grant must produce a usable permission prompt. That case has never been run. It is the entire first-run experience.

THE STRONGEST ARGUMENT FOR A HELPER TURNS OUT NOT TO BE LOCATION. o3a recorded cache_delete terminating the menu bar app 7 times in 8 days, and launch-at-login does not cover mid-session termination. hib.10 demonstrated that a launchd agent, killed outright, comes back on its own. That self-healing property is what neither Option 1 nor Option 2 offers -- and it argues for an agent with no location involvement at all, which is a day of work rather than weeks.

RECOMMENDED SEQUENCE:
  1. Ship e70.53 -- launch-at-login on by default, opt-out. ~1 hour. Closes most of the freshness gap and makes step 2 meaningful.
  2. Observe a week. How often does a Current Location widget still go stale with the app actually resident? Nobody has that number, so every estimate of Option 3's value right now is a guess.
  3. If o3a bites in the wild, build the WATCHDOG, not the epic -- a launchd agent whose only job is relaunching the main app. No location entitlement, no second TCC identity, no first-run prompt, no migration, no privacy-label change. Verify first that a sandboxed helper can launch a sibling app (unverified), and give it backoff, since the termination assertion blocks relaunch during the purge. ~1 day, and a strict subset of Option 3.
  4. Only then revisit full Option 3, GATED ON the deferred hib.10 question 5: headless launchd-started helper, no grant, fresh bundle id -- does a usable prompt appear? If not, hib.6 is not buildable as written. That spike is a day; the epic is weeks.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THIS -- stated so the recommendation is falsifiable:
  - Step 2 shows widgets still going stale often with the app resident. Most likely thing to flip it.
  - You want data to follow you as you move (significant-location-change monitoring). That needs a resident location owner and is squarely Option 3. Note the macOS relaunch behaviour for that API is itself unverified.
  - Users are expected to quit the app routinely. The whole argument assumes the app is normally resident; if that is wrong, so is the sequencing.
  - You judge a 2.9 MB resident helper versus a full resident app worth the weeks on its own. Legitimate -- just a different case from the one this issue currently makes for itself, and it should be decided on those terms.

ALSO, INDEPENDENT OF THIS DECISION: the agent is killed by SIGKILL, not SIGTERM (launchctl status -9, no exit line despite a handler). Any background writer of the App Group cache must be atomic and interrupt-safe. Applies to the widget and app too, not just a future helper.

comments.author: Steve Barber
comments.text:
CORRECTION to the recommendation above (2026-08-31, same day). The memo has been revised at the same URL; this records what changed and why, because it alters the reasoning rather than just the wording.

WHAT WAS WRONG: I repeatedly said Option 3 "costs weeks" -- in the skeptical design review, in comments on hib.2/hib.5, and in the recommendation. That phrase is VERBATIM FROM THIS ISSUE'S OWN DESCRIPTION, written 2026-08-12. I inherited it and never derived it. A review whose stated job was to question this issue's assumptions should have questioned that one too, and did not.

"WEEKS" WAS THREE DIFFERENT THINGS WEARING ONE WORD:
  - Engineering effort: 3-5 days. The code is small and reuses BluegullAQIKit wholesale -- fetch, cache, keychain and resolver all already work in a non-app process.
  - Calendar time at actual cadence: 2-4 weeks. Grounded, not guessed: git shows 24 active days in the last 60 (~2.8 working days/week), and the mtm epic closed 25 issues across four calendar weeks on that rhythm. hib has eight open.
  - Latency that cannot be compressed: reboots, overnight observation (hib.9's own text says "over hours"), App Review. THIS is what actually made it "weeks," and it is not effort.

EVIDENCE FOR THAT THIRD CATEGORY, from this spike: the whole mechanism was built in about an hour. Then two silent failure modes surfaced -- xcodegen overwriting the entitlements file, and Xcode stripping app-sandbox during packaging -- both of which produced a GREEN BUILD and a subtly broken helper, caught only by inspecting the signature. Then question 4's first answer was wrong for a day and took 29 hours of data to correct. An hour of building, then a day of establishing whether it does what you think. Worse here than usual because the tests are irreversible: the locationd grant cannot be removed, so a botched clean-install test costs a bundle id or a VM rebuild.

THE CORRECTION CUTS AGAINST MY OWN RECOMMENDATION, WHICH IS WHY IT MATTERS: hib.10 did not only answer questions, it BUILT part of the epic. hib.2 (scaffold, fresh bundle id), hib.3 (register via SMAppService.agent) and most of hib.5 (the activity schedule) now exist as working, signed, sandboxed, measured code in spike/hib10/. Three of the eight open issues are substantially done. So the price is lower than this issue's description claims, and the case for waiting must not rest on an inflated one.

WHAT THE RECOMMENDATION NOW RESTS ON INSTEAD: not price, but WHERE THE RISK SITS. What genuinely remains is hib.4 (fetch and cache write, reusing existing code), hib.6/hib.7 (a design contradiction, not typing), hib.8 (migration) and hib.9 (verification). Nearly all residual risk concentrates in the TCC / permission / migration cluster -- exactly where the untested headless first-run prompt lives. Building more of the mechanism does not resolve that unknown, which is why the gate is the question-5 spike (one day) rather than an effort budget.

The recommended sequence is UNCHANGED: ship e70.53, observe a week, build the watchdog if o3a bites, and gate full Option 3 on the question-5 prompt spike. Added to "what would change this": if question 5 shows a clean headless first-run prompt, the main reason to wait evaporates -- and with three issues already built, the remainder is modest. That is the cheapest experiment available and it is a day.

comments.author: Steve Barber
comments.text:
RECOMMENDATION REVERSED (2026-09-01): BUILD IT. Memo rewritten at the same URL -- https://claude.ai/code/artifact/bc1d3f3a-d867-4785-855e-1a3182e72368

WHY IT MOVED, AND WHY THAT IS NOT DRIFT: the previous recommendation set an explicit, falsifiable gate -- "if question 5 shows no usable headless first-run prompt, hib.6 is not buildable as written and the epic needs redesigning." That spike has now run. Prompt drawn 0.2s after the request from a launchd-started process with ppid=1, granted at 5.4s, fix at 35m accuracy, on a bundle id locationd had never seen. The gate is cleared, so the recommendation moves. See hib.10 for the full trace.

BUT THE CASE IS NOT THE EPIC'S OWN CASE. Steve raised the architectural objection and it reframes this correctly: the epic sells Option 3 on a "genuinely on-demand lifecycle," which measurement refuted. Option 3's real value is structural. BlueGull today conflates three roles in one bundle -- UI surface, data owner, and background worker -- so data exists only while a UI process is alive, and every future surface (Shortcuts action, Control Center module, second widget family, CLI) inherits that dependency. hib.6's inversion is the daemon/client split: helper owns location/fetch/cache, menu bar app and widget are both just views onto it, neither privileged, neither required by the other.

Option 2 is the option that accrues debt, because making the menu bar app permanently resident ENTRENCHES the conflation. And the coupling is not hypothetical: o3a is it already failing -- macOS terminates the app to purge its CONTAINER CACHES, a pure UI-process concern, and data freshness dies with it, 7 times in 8 days. Meanwhile hib.10 measured a helper killed outright by jetsam and re-spawned by launchd on its own four minutes later. A data owner should not be killable for UI reasons.

ALSO WORTH RECORDING, since it was the original worry: depending on a background helper is not a hack born of building the menu bar app first. A macOS widget extension CANNOT resolve location (authStatus=0, delegateCallbacks=0, CoreLocation never engages), and Apple's own macOS Weather widget is backed by weatherd, a resident LaunchAgent -- Weather.app need not be running. A survey of this machine found 13 third-party apps bundling helper agents or login items. And the dependency is per-FEATURE, not per-user: pinned-location widgets are already self-sufficient (mtm.24), so only Current Location needs any of this.

RECOMMENDED SEQUENCE (revised -- decisions before code):
  1. Settle hib.6 vs hib.7 on paper. Does the app keep a fallback grant? Migration, degraded mode and the clean-install prompt count all follow from that one answer, which is currently contradictory in the tracker.
  2. Design the first-run MOMENT. Three things the spike proved are needed and hib.6 does not mention: have the app start the helper deliberately when the user enables Current Location (the spike's prompt fired on the system's schedule with someone watching for it -- in production that could be hours after install, mid-task, from an unrecognised process); give the helper a display name the user recognises (the probe's prompt said "BlueGull AQI Location Probe"); and hold an xpc transaction across the human decision, or launchd may reap the helper while the prompt is still on screen.
  3. Promote the spike code and finish hib.4. hib.2/hib.3/most of hib.5 already exist signed, sandboxed and measured in spike/hib10/.
  4. Ship e70.53 alongside -- but as a UI PREFERENCE, not a freshness mechanism. Under decomposition, launch-at-login stops meaning "keep data alive" and becomes "do you want the menu bar icon at login," which is a clean thing to keep. Shipping it WITHOUT the decomposition is what would ossify.
  5. Then hib.8 migration and hib.9 verification.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THIS AGAIN:
  - Settling hib.6 forces a second prompt on a clean install. Two prompts for one feature is a bad first run and would reopen whether the helper should own location at all, versus merely keeping the app alive.
  - App Review pushes back on background location collection. The one cost here not under your control, though the widget limitation is demonstrable.
  - You decide the decomposition is not actually wanted. If a permanently resident menu bar app is fine, Option 2 plus a watchdog is genuinely cheaper -- that is legitimate, it just has to be decided on architectural grounds rather than on freshness numbers.

comments.author: Steve Barber
comments.text:
DECIDED 2026-09-01 (Steve): OPTION 1 -- helper only. The helper is the sole location owner; the app does NOT keep a location grant as a fallback.

Rationale as presented and accepted: an app-side fallback only works while the app is open, but the widget refreshes whether the app is open or not. With the background item switched off, the popover would show fresh AQI and the widget stale AQI for the same "Current Location" -- one feature, two numbers, no signal to the user that anything is wrong. Failing cleanly on both surfaces is the same call already made in dc2.7 and e70.31: an honest "this is old" beats a number quietly pretending to be current.

Costs accepted with the decision: a user who prunes their Login Items list loses Current Location until they re-enable it. Mitigated by pinned locations continuing to work (they need no grant at all), so the product degrades by one feature rather than appearing broken -- and by hib.7's detect-and-explain path, which is now real work rather than an afterthought.

ISSUES UPDATED TO MATCH, contradiction removed:
- hib.6 rewritten. Acceptance is now exactly one prompt, from the HELPER, at a moment the user has just asked for Current Location; no CLLocationManager authorization request from the app at all. Names the concrete app-side changes: BluegullAQIApp.swift:41's LocationPermissionRequester(requestOnInit:) must go, and AQIRefreshController.swift:176/:265 read the cache instead of resolving. Also absorbs the three first-run design points hib.10 question 5 surfaced (prompt timing, helper display name, holding a transaction across the human decision).
- hib.7 retitled "Detect and explain when the helper is disabled, unapproved, or absent" and rescoped from fallback to detection + honest explanation + recovery path. Acceptance now requires both surfaces to agree rather than requiring the app to keep working.
- hib.8 simplified. The old open question about relinquishing the app's grant is answered: neither kept nor relinquished -- it just goes unused, and cannot be removed anyway (locationd, -10814). Remaining real work is the upgrade window before the helper's first successful write, and making sure a declined prompt is explained in terms of the upgrade rather than as a generic error.

Next per the memo's sequence: step 2, design the first-run moment (now folded into hib.6).

title: Menu bar: never display stale data (currently shows readings up to 3h old indistinguishably)
description:
Steve's requirement (2026-08-11), emphatic: 'I never want to show stale data on the menu bar!!! No one will notice it is stale.'

Current behavior is exactly what he is objecting to. MenuBarStatusLabel (AQISummaryComponents.swift:67) renders whatever AQIReading it is handed, with no freshness input at all -- BluegullAQIApp.swift:115 passes only refreshController?.latestReading. AppGroupCache.get() deliberately keeps returning soft-expired readings (past defaultSoftTTL = 3600) right up to defaultHardTTL = 3*3600, so the menu bar can silently show a number up to three hours old that looks identical to a current one. The menu bar is the worst surface for that precisely because it is a single glanceable number with no room for qualification -- exactly Steve's point that nobody will notice.

Note this is the inverse of the widget requirement in the sibling bead: the widget SHOULD show aged data, labelled with an absolute timestamp; the menu bar should NOT show it at all.
design: AQIFreshness (.fresh/.stale/.expired) already exists and is plumbed into WidgetTimelineSnapshot.freshness, but AQIRefreshController does not expose it to the menu bar label -- that plumbing is the bulk of the work. NEEDS A DESIGN DECISION FROM STEVE on what the menu bar shows instead once a reading goes stale: most likely the existing no-data state (the aqi.medium SF Symbol already used when there is no reading), so stale collapses to 'no number' rather than a wrong number. Scope is the menu bar item itself; the popover is a separate surface with room to show an aged reading plus its timestamp, and should probably keep doing so.
acceptance_criteria: Once a reading passes the soft TTL, the menu bar item stops displaying its AQI value. A stale reading is never visually indistinguishable from a fresh one in the menu bar.
close_reason: Implemented in dc1f62f: absolute observation timestamps on widget staleCaption, menu bar never renders soft/hard-expired readings

title: AirNow read timeout raises unhandled TimeoutError -> HTTP 500, bypassing stale-data fallback
description:
Found while diagnosing Steve's widget showing 'Data Unavailable / Last updated 3 hours ago' (2026-08-11). The dev endpoint returned HTTP 500 at 10.3s, then timed out entirely; minutes later the same endpoint served 200s in ~0.1-0.35s.

Root cause, verified end to end:

1. airnow_client.fetch_observations calls urlopen(url, timeout=REQUEST_TIMEOUT_SECONDS) with REQUEST_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 10 (airnow_client.py:50).
2. A read-phase timeout raises builtins.TimeoutError, which is NOT a subclass of urllib.error.URLError. Verified empirically with a local stalling HTTP server, not assumed: 'raised: builtins.TimeoutError / isinstance URLError: False'. (socket.timeout IS TimeoutError as of Python 3.10; service runs python3.14.)
3. fetch_observations catches only HTTPError and URLError (airnow_client.py:52-59), so TimeoutError escapes un-wrapped -- it never becomes AirNowError.
4. aqi_lookup._refresh's stale-first fallback catches AirNowError and RateLimitExceededError only (aqi_lookup.py:127-136). TimeoutError matches neither, so the deliberate 'serve stale when AirNow is unreachable' safety net is bypassed even when perfectly good stale data exists in DynamoDB.
5. lambda_handler catches OutOfCoverageError/AirNowError/RateLimitExceededError with no broad except (lambda_handler.py:44-59), so it propagates out as a Lambda invocation error.
6. API Gateway returns HTTP 500 {"message":"Internal Server Error"} -- note that is API Gateway's generic shape, not this service's own {"error": ...} shape, which is how the failure was identified as escaping the handler's error mapping entirely.

Impact is not just a wrong status code. A timeout is the single most likely way AirNow becomes unreachable, and it is precisely the case that slips past every layer of the intended resilience design: no stale fallback, no 502 mapping, no friendly message. The client (BluegullServiceClient, its own 10s timeout) just sees a 500. The widget's self-fetch failure is silent by design (BluegullAQIWidget.swift), so this surfaces to the user as an unexplained 'Data Unavailable' -- exactly Steve's report.
design: Catch TimeoutError alongside URLError in fetch_observations and wrap it as AirNowError, so it flows through the existing stale-first path in _refresh and the handler's 502 mapping with no other changes. Order matters: HTTPError must stay caught before URLError (it is a subclass). Note both urllib.error.URLError and TimeoutError are subclasses of OSError, so catching OSError would cover both -- but explicit is better here given the secrets rule about never letting the AirNow URL into an exception message.
acceptance_criteria: A read timeout from AirNow returns cached stale data when any exists, and a 502 with the friendly upstream-unavailable message when none does -- never a 500. Regression test covers the timeout path specifically (currently untested); a stalling local HTTP server as used to verify the diagnosis is sufficient.
notes: Deployed to dev 2026-08-11 ~19:35 ET via sam deploy --config-env dev (stack bluegull-aqi-dev, us-east-2). Changeset was two in-place Modify operations (AqiFunction, AqiHttpApi), no replacements. Verified post-deploy: cold invoke on a fresh container returned HTTP 200 in 3.1s, reserved concurrency still unset (function enabled, not pinned to 0). The fix is now live.
close_reason: Fixed in 3100b84 on branch fix/airnow-timeout (not yet merged or deployed). Added an 'except TimeoutError' clause to airnow_client.fetch_observations wrapping it as AirNowError, so a read timeout now flows through aqi_lookup._refresh's existing serve-stale fallback and lambda_handler's 502 mapping instead of escaping as an unhandled exception -> API Gateway 500. Message text is static (TimeoutError can carry the socket address; the URL carries API_KEY). Four regression tests added covering the unit wrap, end-to-end serve-stale, the no-stale-data 502 path, and non-leakage of key/address -- all confirmed FAILING on the unfixed code with the exact production error before the fix. Also pinned the structural fact that lambda_handler has no broad except. Full service suite 74 passed, pylint 10/10. NOT yet deployed to dev -- the running Lambda still has the bug.

title: Widget configured to Current Location can show permanent Data Unavailable
description: Steve hit this live (2026-08-12): switched a desktop widget's location to Current Location, got Data Unavailable. Root cause: AQIRefreshController.refreshNow() only calls cache.putCurrentLocation() when the MENU BAR's own selection is nil/current-location (AQIRefreshController.swift:146-148). A placed widget's own configuration is completely independent of the menu bar's selection, and WidgetTimelineComputer.currentSnapshot() for a nil (Current Location) widget config reads exactly that cache slot (cache.getCurrentLocation()) with no fallback fetch -- the widget extension has no location entitlement and explicitly does not attempt to resolve GPS itself for the Current Location case (see BluegullAQIWidget.swift's timeline(for:in:) comment, bluegull-aqi-mtm.24). bluegull-aqi-mtm.24 deleted the old o4b relay (WidgetRequestedLocationsStore/widgetSettleLoop/activeWidgetLocations) that used to enumerate placed widgets and fetch on their behalf, since it was redundant once widgets could self-fetch pinned locations -- but nothing replaced it for the Current Location case, which widgets still can't self-fetch. Net effect: if the menu bar is pinned to a named location (not Current Location), the current-location cache slot never gets refreshed by anything, and any widget configured to Current Location shows Data Unavailable indefinitely -- not intermittent flakiness, a deterministic function of the menu bar's own unrelated selection.
acceptance_criteria: AQIRefreshController's refresh loop keeps the Current Location cache slot fresh every cycle regardless of the menu bar's own selection, so a widget configured to Current Location gets real data within one refresh cycle (not permanently stuck), the same guarantee already provided for pinned locations. Verified against a real placed widget switched to Current Location while the menu bar is pinned to a different location.
close_reason: Fixed AQIRefreshController.refreshNow() to keep the Current Location cache slot (cache.putCurrentLocation) warm every refresh cycle regardless of the menu bar's own selection, resolving GPS at most once per cycle either way. Verified live against the actual root cause: pinned the menu bar to Home (a named location) via 'defaults write solutions.bluegull.aqi menuBarLocationSelection <Home's pin ID>', rebuilt with the fix, relaunched, and confirmed both aqi-cache-current-location and Home's own cache entry got fresh fetchedAt timestamps in the same refresh cycle (previously, only Home's entry would have updated -- current-location would have stayed stale/absent forever under this exact scenario, which is precisely what Steve hit this morning). Restored his menu bar selection back to Current Location afterward. make test-swift passes (174/174; AQIRefreshController itself isn't unit tested, per its own doc comment -- same as before this change).

title: Air Quality Detail window silently truncates the disclaimer
description: Screenshot from Steve, 2026-08-05: the disclaimer text at the bottom of the widget's tap-to-expand detail view cuts off mid-sentence ('...have not been fully verified or v...'). Root cause: WidgetDetailView's Window (id: widget-detail) has its frame persisted by AppKit's own autosave, independent of .windowResizability(.contentSize)'s ideal-size behavior -- a frame saved when the view needed less height (fewer pollutants, or before the disclaimer reached its current length) gets restored as-is on a later launch, and a bare VStack has no way to signal it's been squeezed smaller than its content -- Text just silently truncates with an ellipsis. Confirmed a real saved frame this session: "NSWindow Frame widget-detail" = "... 320 273 ..." and later "... 320 339 ...", both plausible past-content-fit sizes for a shorter reading.
acceptance_criteria: The full disclaimer text is always reachable regardless of the window's current height, past or future.
close_reason: Fixed: wrapped WidgetDetailView's content in a ScrollView instead of a bare VStack, so the compliance-required disclaimer (and everything else in this view) is always at least reachable by scrolling regardless of the window's actual restored height, past or future -- rather than trying to fight or reset AppKit's own frame-autosave, which would just go stale again the next time content grows (more pollutants, longer copy). Also cleared the currently-stale saved frame (NSWindow Frame widget-detail) so the fix is visible immediately on next open rather than requiring a manual resize first. make test-swift passes (11 BluegullAQITests, 184 BluegullAQIKit tests).

title: Productionize widget-side fetching: mode in App Group, remove o4b relay
description: Make the bluegull-aqi-mtm.23 spike shippable (Service mode path). Strip the temporary file logging from BluegullAQIWidget. Move DataSourceModeStore from the container app's UserDefaults.standard into the App Group so the widget can see which mode the user picked -- it currently cannot, because that store was written on the assumption the widget never fetches. Delete the now-redundant bluegull-aqi-o4b scaffolding: WidgetRequestedLocationsStore (+tests), AQIRefreshController.widgetSettleLoop/refreshWidgetLocations/activeWidgetLocations. Measured 2026-08-05: with both the app's settle loop and the widget both fetching, outbound request volume was 2x what's needed (4 app + 4 widget in the same window).
acceptance_criteria: Widget fetches on cache miss in Service mode with no debug logging; widget honors the user's actual DataSourceMode; app no longer fetches on widgets' behalf; re-measured outbound request volume shows the duplication gone. make test-swift green.
close_reason:
Implemented. Stripped spike logging; moved DataSourceModeStore into the App Group (with migrateFromStandardIfNeeded so an existing Direct-mode choice doesn't silently revert, called from BluegullAQIApp.init before the fetch loop starts); deleted WidgetRequestedLocationsStore + its 9 tests, AQIRefreshController.widgetSettleLoop, refreshWidgetLocations, and activeWidgetLocations. Kept a single WidgetCenter.reloadTimelines after a successful menu-bar fetch (at most once per refresh, vs the settle loop's every 20s) so a widget on the same location isn't stuck behind its own reload policy. Updated doc/DESIGN.md: corrected the 'container app owns all networking' and 'does not fetch network or location itself' statements, flagged that App Attest cannot run in a WidgetKit extension and so must be settled before adoption, and added a changelog entry. Historical dated changelog entries left intact.

Verified: duplication gone -- same clear-two-locations scenario went from 8 outbound requests (4 app + 4 widget) to 2, with Cleveland and Boston each fetched exactly once. 168 tests pass (12 BluegullAQITests + 156 BluegullAQIKit; net -9 deleted relay tests, +7 new DataSourceModeStore tests covering read, fallback, unavailable-suite, and all three migration cases).

title: SPIKE: let the widget extension fetch directly on cache miss (Service mode)
description:
Time-boxed spike to validate the core thesis of Steve's 2026-08-05 shared-cache/refresh design doc: that the widget extension should fetch for itself rather than depending on the container app, which is the root cause of the 3-5 minute delay when configuring a widget to a new location (bluegull-aqi-mtm.22).

Evidence the thesis is right, from the 2026-08-04 session logs: the widget extension process DOES receive its correct configured location promptly and in-process ('intent = { location = { title = Syracuse } }' followed by a successful timeline request, milliseconds after configuration), while the cross-process WidgetCenter.getCurrentConfigurations() query returns nil (bluegull-aqi-o4b). Everything built in o4b -- WidgetRequestedLocationsStore, the 20s widgetSettleLoop, the reloadTimelines nudge -- is scaffolding to route a fact the widget already knows back to the only process allowed to act on it.

doc/DESIGN.md:193 justifies the current split as 'WidgetKit extensions have restricted background networking.' That appears to conflate the background refresh budget (real; governs how often WidgetKit invokes a provider unprompted) with network access while the provider is running (not restricted; widget extensions can make URLSession calls in getTimeline). A configuration change is a user-initiated trigger, not a background-budget event.

Backend latency measured 2026-08-05 and is NOT the bottleneck: https://dev.aqi.bluegull.solutions/aqi returns 200 in 311ms cold / 122ms warm for Chicago. The 1-2s responsiveness target is achievable if the widget can fetch at all.

Service mode only for the spike -- it is already Steve's actual mode (DataSourceMode.defaultMode == .service, no override key set), and it needs no credential, so the measurement isolates the latency question from Keychain/entitlement plumbing.
acceptance_criteria: Add com.apple.security.network.client to the widget extension target; have the widget's TimelineProvider fetch via AQIFetchCoordinator on an exact cache miss and return the fresh value in the same timeline. Then measure, on a real placed widget: configure it to a brand-new uncached location and record wall-clock time until the value appears. Success is a value on screen in roughly 1-2 seconds instead of minutes. If it succeeds, follow-on work is Keychain access-group sharing so Direct mode gets the same path (Steve approved 2026-08-05), mirroring DataSourceMode into the App Group so the widget can see which mode is selected, and deleting the now-redundant o4b relay/poll scaffolding.
close_reason: Spike succeeded and is productionized in bluegull-aqi-mtm.24. Result: widget-side fetch on cache miss took 0.343s for Cleveland, a brand-new location Steve configured through Edit Widget, versus 3-5 minutes on the old relay architecture; Steve confirmed 'less than a second' subjectively. Also validated the design doc's reliability goal -- a run with zero container-app processes fetched and cached Boston Metro successfully. Backend was never the bottleneck (122-311ms). Incidentally surfaced bluegull-aqi-10h.21, a P0 decode bug that made Boston permanently unavailable in every configuration.

title: make test-swift launched the real app for real, re-triggering the Location permission dialog and a real network fetch every run
